title: 04 — The Data Lakehouse
html:
04 — The Data Lakehouse

The one idea: a lakehouse is a data lake whose files are organised into real tables — with transactions, schemas, history and access control — by an open table format and a catalog. You get warehouse behaviour (reliable SQL tables) at lake cost (cheap object storage, open files, any engine).

1. Definition

A data lakehouse is an architecture in which:

  1. Data is stored in open file formats (usually Apache Parquet) on object storage you own.
  2. An open table format (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake or Apache Hudi) adds a metadata layer that turns sets of files into tables with ACID transactions, schema enforcement and evolution, time travel and row-level updates and deletes.
  3. A catalog names the tables, points each name at its current metadata, and enforces permissions.
  4. Many compute engines — Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, Polars, Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery … — read and write the same tables, with no copy into a proprietary store.

2. How we got here

Generation What it is Strength Weakness
Data warehouse (1990s → ) Database built for analytics; data loaded into its own storage Fast SQL, ACID, governance Expensive, proprietary storage, poor for unstructured data and ML, one engine
Data lake (2010s) Files dumped in HDFS / object storage, schema applied at read Cheap, any data type, any engine No transactions, no reliable updates, "data swamp", inconsistent reads during writes
Lake + warehouse (two-tier) Lake for raw, copy curated data into a warehouse Each tier does what it is good at Two copies, two security models, ETL lag, drift between them
Lakehouse (2020s) Table format + catalog on the lake One copy, open, transactional, multi-engine You operate maintenance (compaction, cleanup) and choose a catalog

The underlying problem a table format solves: on plain object storage, a reader listing s3://lake/sales/ while a writer is adding 200 files sees an arbitrary subset. There is no "commit". A table format writes data files first and then publishes one atomic metadata change that says "the table now consists of these files".

3. The layers of a lakehouse

Layer Responsibility Examples
Storage Durable bytes S3, ADLS Gen2, GCS, MinIO
File format Efficient columnar encoding of rows Parquet (also ORC, Avro)
Table format Which files form the table, at which version; schema; partitioning; transactions Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi
Catalog Table names → current metadata; namespaces; permissions; credential vending Lakekeeper, Apache Polaris, Unity Catalog, Nessie, AWS Glue, Hive Metastore
Engines Plan and execute queries and writes Spark, Trino, Flink, DuckDB, Polars, Snowflake, Databricks

4. How data is actually stored

A single Iceberg table on disk:

s3://warehouse/silver/nav/
├── metadata/
│   ├── 00000-3a1f….metadata.json        ← table metadata, version 0
│   ├── 00001-7bc2….metadata.json        ← version 1 (after first append)
│   ├── 00002-91de….metadata.json        ← current version
│   ├── snap-6114…-1-….avro              ← manifest list for one snapshot
│   ├── 8c3e…-m0.avro                    ← manifest: list of data files + column stats
│   └── 8c3e…-m1.avro
└── data/
    ├── nav_month=2026-09/
    │   ├── 00000-0-….parquet
    │   └── 00001-0-….parquet
    └── nav_month=2026-10/
        └── 00000-1-….parquet
  • Data files are ordinary Parquet. You could open one with DuckDB directly — but you should not, because only the metadata knows which files are live.
  • Metadata is JSON (table-level) and Avro (manifests). It is small relative to data.
  • The catalog stores one fact per table: "the current metadata file is 00002-91de….metadata.json". Changing that pointer is the commit.

Chapter 05 walks through each file.

4.1 Parquet in one paragraph

Parquet stores a file as row groups (e.g. 128 MB of rows), each split into column chunks, each split into pages. Every column chunk carries min/max/null-count statistics, so a reader can skip row groups whose range cannot match a filter. Columns are encoded (dictionary, run-length, delta) and compressed (Snappy, Zstd). Result: reading two columns of a 50-column table reads roughly 4% of the bytes. More in Storage formats and layout.

5. Table formats compared

Apache Iceberg Delta Lake Apache Hudi
Origin Netflix → Apache Databricks → Linux Foundation Uber → Apache
Metadata Tree: metadata JSON → manifest list → manifests Ordered JSON log + Parquet checkpoints in _delta_log/ Timeline of instants in .hoodie/
Partitioning Hidden, with transforms; partition layout can evolve Explicit columns; liquid clustering as alternative Explicit
Schema evolution By field ID — rename and reorder are safe By name (column mapping mode adds IDs) Supported
Row-level changes Copy-on-write or merge-on-read (delete files, deletion vectors in v3) Copy-on-write; deletion vectors Copy-on-write or merge-on-read; strong upsert/indexing focus
Catalog Pluggable; REST catalog spec is the open standard Unity Catalog / Hive / path-based Hive metastore and others
Engine support Broadest: Spark, Trino, Flink, Dremio, Snowflake, BigQuery, Athena, DuckDB, PyIceberg … Best inside Databricks; good in Spark, delta-rs, DuckDB Spark and Flink centred

Convergence: Delta UniForm can expose Delta tables as Iceberg metadata; Iceberg v3 adopted deletion vectors and a variant type. In practice, choose Iceberg when multi-engine openness and an independent catalog matter, Delta when you are mainly on Databricks. The Delta Lake chapter covers Delta in depth.

6. The medallion architecture

A layering convention, not a technology: each layer has a contract about quality.

Layer Contains Rules Typical writes
Landing Original files (chapter 03) Byte-identical, hashed, WORM Collector only
Bronze Parsed records, close to source shape Every row traceable to a file; no business logic; append-only Append
Silver Validated, typed, de-duplicated, conformed, entity-resolved Passed the quality gate; canonical IDs; bitemporal history Append + merge
Gold Business-ready, certified aggregates and features Reviewed and signed off; stable semantics Overwrite by partition or append new vintage 
---
title: Medallion flow with gates
---
flowchart LR
    L["Landing<br/>raw files"] -->|parse| B["Bronze<br/>raw records"]
    B -->|"quality gate<br/>(contracts)"| S["Silver<br/>validated, conformed"]
    B -->|fail| Q["Quarantine"]
    S -->|"curate + human sign-off"| G["Gold<br/>certified"]
    G --> C["Consumers<br/>BI, models, APIs, agents"]

Rules of thumb:

  • Consumers read Gold (or Silver for exploration), never Bronze.
  • Each layer can be rebuilt from the one before it. Landing is the only thing you cannot rebuild — hence WORM.
  • Promote with atomic commits: a batch either appears entirely in Silver or not at all (one Iceberg commit).

7. How to build one — the minimum local lakehouse

You need four things: object storage, a catalog, a table format library, and an engine.

# compose.yaml — local lakehouse
services:
  minio:
    image: minio/minio
    command: server /data --console-address ":9001"
    environment: { MINIO_ROOT_USER: admin, MINIO_ROOT_PASSWORD: password123 }
    ports: ["9000:9000", "9001:9001"]

  postgres:                               # catalog's own database
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: catalog, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: catalog, POSTGRES_DB: catalog }

  catalog:                                # an Iceberg REST catalog — see chapter 07 for real settings
    image: quay.io/lakekeeper/catalog:latest
    depends_on: [postgres, minio]
    ports: ["8181:8181"]

Then, in Python (chapter 06 explains every line):

from pyiceberg.catalog import load_catalog
from datetime import date
from decimal import Decimal
import pyarrow as pa

catalog = load_catalog("lake", type="rest", uri="http://localhost:8181/catalog", warehouse="demo")
catalog.create_namespace_if_not_exists("silver")

data = pa.table({"isin": ["INF209K01YN0"], "nav_date": [date(2026, 10, 31)],
                 "nav": pa.array([Decimal("123.4567")], pa.decimal128(18, 4))})
table = catalog.create_table_if_not_exists("silver.nav", schema=data.schema)
table.append(data)

print(table.scan().to_polars())

That is a working lakehouse: Parquet files in MinIO, Iceberg metadata, a REST catalog, and two engines (PyIceberg and Polars) reading the same table. Add DuckDB or Spark and they see the same data.

8. How you work with a lakehouse day to day

Task How
Create a table Engine DDL (CREATE TABLE … USING iceberg) or PyIceberg create_table
Load data Append (new rows), overwrite by filter (replace a partition), merge/upsert (change rows)
Query Any engine that knows the catalog
Look at the past Time travel by snapshot ID, timestamp, or tag
Change schema Add/rename/drop columns — metadata-only, no rewrite
Change partitioning Partition evolution — new data uses the new layout
Keep it fast Compaction (rewrite_data_files), sort/cluster, rewrite manifests
Keep it cheap Expire old snapshots, delete orphan files
Secure it Catalog permissions per namespace/table; credential vending so engines never hold long-lived storage keys
Share it Give another engine or organisation catalog access — no export

9. Trade-offs and pitfalls

  • Small files. Streaming or frequent small appends create thousands of tiny files; query planning and reads slow down. Schedule compaction.
  • Metadata growth. Every commit adds a snapshot. Expire snapshots you do not need (but keep tagged ones).
  • Catalog is critical infrastructure. If the catalog is down, nobody can commit. Back up its database.
  • Concurrent writers use optimistic concurrency: one wins, others retry. Design jobs so two writers rarely touch the same partition.
  • Not an OLTP database. Commits take hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. Do not use a lakehouse table as an application's transactional store.

10. If you come from .NET and SQL Server

Lakehouse SQL Server analogy
Parquet file A data file (.mdf/.ndf) — but immutable and readable by any tool
Table format metadata Transaction log + system catalog views
Snapshot A database snapshot / a point in the log
Catalog The sys.* catalog plus logins and permissions
Compaction Index rebuild
Engines Many independent query processors sharing one set of files

11. Questions to test yourself

  1. What exactly does a table format add on top of Parquet files in a bucket?
  2. Why is a reader of a plain data lake able to see half-written data, and how does an Iceberg commit prevent it?
  3. Which medallion layer is the only one that cannot be rebuilt, and why?
  4. List three operational jobs a lakehouse needs that a managed warehouse does for you.
  5. When would you pick Delta Lake over Iceberg?

12. Review checklist

  • Storage, table format, catalog and engines are chosen explicitly.
  • Every table belongs to a medallion layer with a written quality contract.
  • Promotion between layers is one atomic commit per batch.
  • Compaction and snapshot expiry are scheduled.
  • Catalog database is backed up; storage credentials are vended, not shared.
